keyVerseText: Ye are the salt of the earth: but if the salt have lost his savour, wherewith shall it be salted? it is thenceforth good for nothing, but to be cast out, and to be trodden under foot of men.
rootMeaning: The Greek adverb ἔτι (éti) is possibly related to the noun ἔτος (étos), meaning 'year.' This connection suggests a root sense of ongoing time or duration, emphasizing continuity or something that extends beyond a certain point. Unlike the English glosses such as 'yet' or 'still,' this root sense highlights the idea of persistence or extension through time, which enriches its temporal and qualitative nuances in Scripture.
usageInScripture: With 101 occurrences, ἔτι is most frequently translated as 'yet,' appearing 35 times, but also commonly as 'more,' 'any more,' and 'still.' This variety shows its flexibility in expressing both temporal continuation and degree, whether referring to the present, past, or future. The word can indicate something that remains in effect, something additional, or something no longer continuing when used with a negation. Its broad range reveals a nuanced function in the biblical text to communicate ongoing states or conditions.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding ἔτι deepens our grasp of biblical temporality and persistence, which are central to the Christian faith. It conveys the enduring nature of God's promises and grace, emphasizing that certain divine realities continue 'yet' or 'still' despite circumstances. This adverb also reminds believers of the ongoing call to faithfulness and the reality of transformation over time. Recognizing its use with negatives highlights the sobering truth of what may cease, urging vigilance in spiritual life. Thus, ἔτι encapsulates both hope in God's unchanging faithfulness and the urgency of response.
keyVerseReflection: In Matthew 5:13, Jesus declares, 'Ye are the salt of the earth: but if the salt have lost his savour, wherewith shall it be salted? it is thenceforth good for nothing...' The implied contrast with ἔτι (yet) underscores the critical moment when salt no longer retains its flavor—it no longer serves its purpose 'any more.' This word's meaning enriches the warning by emphasizing the loss of continuing effectiveness, urging believers to maintain their distinctiveness and influence in the world as salt that still has savor.
